label: Measure RTM
title: Bay Area transit sales tax
official: Connect Bay Area Transit Initiative (Regional Measure RTM)
area: Every voter in Santa Clara, San Mateo, San Francisco, Alameda, and Contra Costa counties
threshold: Simple majority of the combined vote across all five counties (not county by county)
short: A 0.5% sales tax in Santa Clara County for 14 years to fund BART, Caltrain, VTA, and other transit.
what: Adds a 0.5% sales tax in Santa Clara, San Mateo, Alameda, and Contra Costa counties, and 1% in San Francisco, for 14 years. It would raise about $980 million a year region-wide for transit operations, plus some road repaving, fare discounts, accessibility, and wayfinding. State law SB 63 (2025) authorized the district; the measure qualified by voter petition.
yes: A new 0.5% sales tax would apply to purchases in Santa Clara County for 14 years, with the money going to regional transit and related road repairs.
no: No new regional transit sales tax. Transit agencies would rely on existing funding.
yesNoSrc: Plain-language summary based on the ballot question. The official wording is in your county voter guide.
fiscal: About $980 million a year region-wide. GrowSF estimates about $290 million a year from Santa Clara County in the first full year (FY 2028).
short_term: Sales tax in Santa Clara County rises by half a cent. Supporters say it prevents major BART, Caltrain, and Muni service cuts. BART has said it would cut train hours sharply starting January 2027 if the measure fails.
long_term: Funding for 14 years, then the tax expires unless renewed. Independent efficiency reviews of BART, Muni, Caltrain, and AC Transit, with funding that can be withheld for poor performance.
supporters: State Sens. Scott Wiener and Jesse Arreguín; Rep. Nancy Pelosi; Chris Larsen; SEIU Local 1021 (per KQED)
opponents: Former Sens. Steve Glazer and Quentin Kopp; former BART director Debora Allen; Contra Costa and San Francisco taxpayer associations (per KQED)
pro: Transit is vital to the region's economy, environment, and quality of life. Agencies face a severe budget crisis from pandemic-era drops in ridership and revenue, and without new money would have to make major cuts, such as eliminating two BART lines.
con: Agencies already receive about $6 billion a year from taxes, tolls, and grants. They should cut costs first, by redirecting capital funds, renegotiating labor contracts, reducing overtime, and automating, and come back later with a smaller tax.
argSrc: KQED Voter Guide summary of each side's case
deep: Santa Clara County spending plan (GrowSF estimates, first full year about $290M): county transportation agency 84.37% (~$245M), which may also go to road repaving; Caltrain 10.38% (~$30M); fare programs 2.78%; accessibility 1.11%; mapping and wayfinding 1.11%; MTC administration 0.25%. Opponents (Fixes Before Funding) argue fixed percentages written into law limit flexibility. These are campaign and advocacy figures; the binding split is in SB 63.

Why a simple majority: it was placed on the ballot by voter petition. Under court rulings since 2017, citizen-initiated special taxes pass with a majority. Prop 43 on the state ballot would require two-thirds for such taxes, but only starting January 1, 2027, so it would not apply to RTM.
Sales taxes take a larger share of income from lower-income households, a point raised in the League of Women Voters' pros and cons.

VTA's history: in 2024 VTA opposed an earlier version of the regional bill (SB 1031), citing concern that Santa Clara County revenue might not return to the county and the effect on renewing local transit taxes. VTA's current Measure A half-cent tax (2000) expires in 2036.
Marin, Napa, Sonoma, and Solano are not in the district and would not pay the tax.

links: League of Women Voters pros & cons (PDF)

reading.source: Local News Matters (Bay City News Foundation)
reading.title: Santa Clara County ballot, Nov. 3, 2026

faq.q: How much more would I pay?
faq.a: The sales tax in Santa Clara County would go up by 0.5%, which is 50 cents on a $100 purchase, for 14 years. Like other California sales taxes, it would not apply to most groceries or prescription medicine.
faq.src: Ballot question; state sales tax rules

faq.q: Where would Santa Clara County's share go?
faq.a: GrowSF estimates the county would raise about $290 million in the first full year. About 84% would go to the county transportation agency, which can also use some of it to repave roads, and about 10% to Caltrain. The rest would go to fare discounts, accessibility, and maps and signs. The binding split is set in state law (SB 63).
faq.src: GrowSF estimates; SB 63

faq.q: Why does it need only a simple majority?
faq.a: It reached the ballot by voter petition, and courts have ruled that special taxes proposed by voters pass with a simple majority. The count is a single combined vote across all five counties, not county by county.
faq.src: Ballot information; KQED

faq.a: The League of Women Voters notes that BART, Muni, Caltrain, and AC Transit face combined operating deficits of more than $800 million a year. The agencies warn of less frequent service, station closures, higher fares, and shorter hours without new money. Opponents argue the agencies could close the gap with savings and existing funds.
faq.src: League of Women Voters of the Bay Area; KQED

faq.a: An independent oversight committee would check that money is spent according to the SB 63 plan. BART, Muni, Caltrain, and AC Transit would get independent efficiency reviews and could have part of their funding withheld if they don't respond. A county could also convene a review committee to withhold funds from an agency that falls short on fares, service, cleanliness, or maintenance.
faq.src: League of Women Voters of the Bay Area

faq.q: Would state Prop 43 change the vote needed?
faq.a: No. Prop 43 would require two-thirds for voter-proposed local special taxes, but only starting January 1, 2027, so it does not apply to RTM.
faq.src: LAO analysis of Prop 43

faq.q: What about counties that aren't included?
faq.a: Marin, Napa, Sonoma, and Solano are outside the district and would not pay the tax. Golden Gate Transit would receive a small share, 0.40% of the money collected in San Francisco.
faq.src: League of Women Voters of the Bay Area

label: Measure O
title: Alum Rock school parcel tax
official: Measure O — Alum Rock Union Elementary School District
area: Voters in the Alum Rock Union Elementary School District (East San José)
threshold: Two-thirds (66.67%), the rule for school parcel taxes
short: Replaces the current $214.10 parcel tax with $310 per parcel per year for 7 years for Alum Rock elementary schools.
what: Replaces the district's current parcel tax of $214.10 per parcel a year, approved in 2022, with a flat $310 per parcel for seven years starting July 1, 2027. It would raise about $6.5 million a year for services for students with disabilities, core academics, teacher recruitment and retention, and students experiencing housing instability.
yes: The current $214.10 parcel tax would be replaced with a $310 per parcel tax for seven years.
no: The current $214.10 parcel tax, approved in 2022, would stay in place until it expires.
yesNoSrc: Plain-language summary based on the ballot question. Check the impartial analysis in your county voter guide.
fiscal: $310 per parcel per year for 7 years, raising about $6.5 million a year, up from about $4.5 million under the current tax.
short_term: Starting July 1, 2027, the annual charge on property tax bills in the district rises from $214.10 to $310 per parcel.
long_term: Expires after seven years unless renewed.
opponents: Silicon Valley Taxpayers Association (per the Mercury News)
deep: A flat parcel tax charges every parcel the same amount regardless of property value, unlike a bond, which is repaid through a rate on assessed value.
Exemptions for homeowners over 65 and people receiving Supplemental Security Income for a disability (Mercury News). Funds cannot go to administrators' salaries.

Background (Mercury News, citing a June 2026 county civil grand jury report): enrollment fell about 39% over the past decade, and the district closed six schools for 2025–26 after a budget shortfall reached $20 million.
This would be the district's fourth parcel tax since 2010.
Read together with Measure P, a bond on the same ballot from the same district.

links: Hoodline, summarizing Mercury News reporting on Measures O and P

reading.source: Local News Matters (Bay City News Foundation)
reading.title: Santa Clara County ballot, Nov. 3, 2026

faq.a: No, it replaces an existing one. Alum Rock already has a parcel tax of $214.10 per parcel a year, which voters approved in 2022. Measure O would replace it with a $310 tax, an increase of $95.90 a year per parcel, for seven years.
faq.src: Ballot question; Mercury News, via Hoodline

faq.a: The current $214.10 tax stays in place until it expires. Voters approved it in 2022 for seven years.
faq.src: Ballotpedia (2022 measure)

faq.q: What would the money pay for?
faq.a: Services for students with disabilities; reading, writing, math, and science programs; recruiting and keeping qualified teachers; and support for students experiencing housing instability. The Mercury News reports the money cannot be used for administrators' salaries.
faq.src: Ballot question; Mercury News, via Hoodline

faq.a: Yes. Seniors can apply for an exemption. The Mercury News reports that homeowners over 65 and people receiving Supplemental Security Income for a disability qualify. Exemptions are handled through the district.
faq.src: Ballot question; Mercury News, via Hoodline

faq.q: How much would it raise, and when?
faq.a: About $6.5 million a year, starting July 1, 2027. The current tax was estimated to raise about $4.5 million a year.
faq.src: Ballot question; Mercury News; Ballotpedia

faq.q: How is it different from Measure P?
faq.a: Both are from the same district and are voted on separately. Measure O (two-thirds needed) pays for programs and staff. Measure P (55% needed) is a $100 million bond for building repairs. Either can pass without the other.
faq.src: Ballot question

label: Measure P
title: Alum Rock school repair bond
official: Measure P — Alum Rock Union Elementary School District
area: Voters in the Alum Rock Union Elementary School District (East San José)
threshold: 55%, the rule for school facilities bonds
short: $100 million in bonds to repair roofs, plumbing, HVAC, and security systems.
what: Authorizes $100 million in bonds for school facilities: repairing roofs and plumbing, replacing heating, ventilation, and air conditioning, and upgrading emergency communication and security systems. Repaid by property owners in the district.
yes: The district could borrow $100 million for school repairs, repaid through property taxes in the district.
no: The district could not issue these bonds.
yesNoSrc: Plain-language summary based on the ballot question as listed by BallotReady.
fiscal: Average levy under $26 per $100,000 of assessed value, raising about $6.3 million a year while bonds are outstanding. The ballot question says current tax rates would not increase.
short_term: Repairs funded as bonds are sold.
long_term: Property owners repay the bonds for as long as they are outstanding, typically decades.
opponents: Silicon Valley Taxpayers Association (per the Mercury News)
deep: "Current tax rates would not increase" usually means the new bonds are timed to replace older bonds as they are paid off. Without the measure, the rate could fall as old bonds retire.
Includes audits, independent oversight, and spending disclosure, as required for school bonds passed at 55%.
Average rate of about $25.52 per $100,000 of assessed value, about $6.3 million a year through 2054. Total repayment about $170 million including interest (Mercury News).

The Mercury News reported the district spent $52.9 million in bond funds from 2021–22 through 2024–25 without a functioning citizens' bond oversight committee. The district says it will establish one if the measures pass.
Prior district bonds: Measure G ($179M, 2008), Measure J ($125M, 2012), Measure I ($140M, 2016), Measure S ($71.5M, 2022).
Read together with Measure O, a parcel tax from the same district.

links: Hoodline, summarizing Mercury News reporting on Measures O and P

reading.source: Local News Matters (Bay City News Foundation)
reading.title: Santa Clara County ballot, Nov. 3, 2026

faq.q: Will my property taxes go up?
faq.a: The ballot question says it would not increase current tax rates. In practice that usually means the new bonds are timed to replace older bonds as they are paid off, so the school bond portion of your bill stays about where it is instead of falling. The average levy would be about $25.52 per $100,000 of assessed value. On a home assessed at $600,000, that is about $153 a year.
faq.src: Ballot question; Mercury News, via Hoodline

faq.q: How long would we pay, and what is the total cost?
faq.a: About $6.3 million a year through 2054. With interest, the total repaid would be about $170 million on $100 million borrowed.
faq.src: Mercury News, via Hoodline

faq.a: Repairing leaky roofs and plumbing, replacing heating, ventilation, and air conditioning, and upgrading emergency communication and security systems. The Mercury News reports the full project list also includes classrooms, restrooms, play areas, cafeterias, and athletic facilities.
faq.src: Ballot question; Mercury News, via Hoodline

faq.a: Bonds passed at 55% legally require a citizens' oversight committee and annual audits. The Mercury News reported the district spent $52.9 million in bond money from 2021–22 through 2024–25 without a functioning oversight committee, and says it will set one up if the measures pass.
faq.src: State law; Mercury News, via Hoodline

faq.a: School facilities bonds can pass with 55% if they include accountability rules such as a project list, audits, and an oversight committee. That rule comes from a 2000 state ballot measure, also called Prop 39, which is different from Prop 39 on this ballot.
faq.src: State law

faq.q: Has the district passed bonds before?
faq.a: Yes, four since 2008: Measure G ($179 million, 2008), Measure J ($125 million, 2012), Measure I ($140 million, 2016), and Measure S ($71.5 million, 2022).
faq.src: Mercury News, via Hoodline

label: Measure Q
title: Cambrian school parcel tax
area: Voters in the Cambrian School District (parts of San José and Campbell)
short: $148 per parcel per year for 8 years for Cambrian elementary and middle schools.
what: A parcel tax of $148 per parcel per year for eight years, adjusted yearly for inflation, for core academics, teacher recruitment and retention, class sizes, and counseling. Funds cannot pay administrator salaries.
yes: Property owners in the district would pay $148 per parcel per year for eight years, starting in 2027–28.
yesNoSrc: Plain-language summary based on the district's Measure Q page.
fiscal: About $1 million a year, kept by the district.
long_term: Eight years, adjusted for inflation each year.
deep: Covers Bagby, Fammatre, Farnham, Price Middle, and Steindorf STEAM Magnet schools.
Homeowners 65 and older can apply for an exemption.
Annual independent audits and public reporting.
The district's page does not say whether Measure Q replaces its 2018 parcel tax (Measure H).

reading.source: Local News Matters (Bay City News Foundation)

faq.a: $148 per parcel a year, about $12.33 a month, adjusted each year for inflation, for eight years. It would first be collected in the 2027–28 fiscal year.

faq.a: Yes. Every parcel, residential or commercial, pays the same flat amount regardless of its value.

label: Measure R
title: Orchard school parcel tax
area: Voters in the Orchard School District (North San José)
short: 4¢ per building square foot, up to $89 per home, for 8 years.
what: A parcel tax of 4 cents per building square foot, capped at $89 per residential parcel and $7,500 per commercial parcel, for eight years starting July 1, 2027. For teacher and staff retention, core academics, STEAM, student mental health, and instructional materials.
yes: Property owners in the district would pay up to $89 per home per year for eight years.
yesNoSrc: Plain-language summary based on the district's announcement.
deep: Exemptions for qualifying seniors and some SSI and SSDI recipients.
Separate account, annual expenditure reports, and an independent audit.

reading.source: Local News Matters (Bay City News Foundation)

faq.q: What would the money pay for?
faq.a: Keeping teachers and staff, STEAM education (science, technology, engineering, arts, and math), visual and performing arts, student mental health, and instructional materials.
